traveler: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley (born Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin)
title: The Hideous Progeny: the Six Weeks' Tour, the Year Without a Summer, and the Editor of the Dead
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Somers Town, the birth and the death eleven days after
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the Polygon at Somers Town a daughter is born to William Godwin, who has argued in print that government must wither away, and to Mary Wollstonecraft, who has argued that women are not made to be ornaments. The afterbirth does not come away whole. Eleven days later the mother is dead of puerperal fever and the philosopher is left with an infant and a three-year-old who is not his. He hangs his wife's portrait over the desk, teaches the girl to read out of her own mother's books, and takes her to spell the name on the stone at St Pancras.
suggested_refs: The site of 29 The Polygon, Somers Town, demolished; the ground now lies near Werrington Street
John Opie's portrait of Mary Wollstonecraft, kept over Godwin's desk

stops.name: Skinner Street, the house over the Juvenile Library
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1807; the pool gives no month for the move
stops.campa: Godwin moves the household to 41 Skinner Street, above the children's publishing business he runs at a loss beside the Fleet ditch, in a street he cannot afford in a trade he does not understand. Mary grows up here with Fanny Imlay, her mother's daughter by an American speculator, and Claire Clairmont, brought in by the stepmother Godwin married in 1801. The family story has the girl hidden behind the sofa to hear Coleridge read The Rime of the Ancient Mariner aloud. The creditors call oftener than the poets. She reads everything in the shop.
suggested_refs: 41 Skinner Street and the sign of the Juvenile Library, M. J. Godwin and Co.

stops.name: Dundee, the Baxters on the Tay
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1812; the sources fix the year and the two visits, not the day of arrival
stops.campa: Godwin sends her north by sea to the house of William Baxter, a radical merchant with daughters her own age, for her health and for the peace of a household grown too full. She stays on the Tay across two visits totalling some sixteen months, walks the firth, and writes. It is the first landscape she has without her father standing in it. She is fourteen and reading Coleridge, and the bare northern coast under a low sky is the country she will hand, years later, to a sea captain writing home to his sister from the ice.
suggested_refs: The Baxter house at The Cottage, Broughty Ferry, near Dundee

stops.name: Skinner Street, the disciple at the table
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1812; the sources disagree on whether this falls before or between the Dundee stays, and the day of any first meeting is not recorded
stops.campa: Percy Bysshe Shelley, twenty, sent down from Oxford for a pamphlet on the necessity of atheism, married to Harriet Westbrook, and writing to Godwin as to a living oracle, dines in Skinner Street in November. Mary is fifteen and home from Scotland. Nothing is set down of what passes. The poet keeps coming, and keeps lending: an obligation of money runs from him to the father before anything runs to the daughter. When the two of them go off together in the spring of 1814, they go from ground Godwin prepared himself and will never pardon.
suggested_refs: Godwin's diary entries recording Shelley's visits to Skinner Street, 1812-1814

stops.name: St Pancras Old Church, at the mother's stone
stops.date_confidence: the meeting on 26 June 1814 is attested in Godwin's diary; the declaration over the tombstone is biographical tradition built afterwards from the diary and Shelley's verse
stops.campa: Mary Wollstonecraft lies under a flat stone in the churchyard, and her daughter has been coming here to read since she could read. On the twenty-sixth of June she comes with Shelley, Claire posted at a distance to keep watch. What the documents hold is that the two of them are here on that day. What the century afterwards holds is the scene: a girl of sixteen declaring herself over her mother's grave to a married man who has told her that the affections cannot be owned. Within a month the house in Skinner Street is broken.
suggested_refs: The flat tomb of Mary Wollstonecraft in St Pancras Old Churchyard, later emptied for the Bournemouth reburial

stops.name: Dover, the boat hired at night
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They leave London before dawn on the hottest day in years: Mary sixteen, Claire brought along because she has the French, Shelley leaving a pregnant wife behind him. At Dover they will not wait for the packet. A boat is hired for the night crossing, a squall comes up in the dark, the little vessel labours, and Mary lies with her head on Shelley's knee while the boatmen work. Dawn shows them the French coast. The journal begun this night will be kept, with breaks and silences, for the rest of her life.
stops.quote: We left London July 28th, 1814, on a hotter day than has been known in this climate for many years.
stops.quote_source: Mary and Percy Shelley, History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), Part I, opening lines
suggested_refs: Dover harbour and the cliffs, point of departure of the 1814 elopement
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), Project Gutenberg eBook 52790

stops.name: Calais, the stepmother at the inn
stops.date_confidence: attested; the crossing is made in the night of 28 July and the landing at dawn on the 29th
stops.campa: They land at dawn and take rooms at Dessin's. That evening a stout Englishwoman comes off the packet asking for her daughter: Mary Jane Godwin has crossed the Channel to fetch Claire home and spends a night working on her. In the morning Claire tells her mother she is going on. The three walk out of Calais and leave her in the inn yard. The household she goes back to is never mended. Godwin does not write to his daughter for two and a half years, and goes on taking Shelley's money the whole time.
suggested_refs: Dessin's hotel at Calais, standard first stop of the English crossing
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817)

stops.name: Paris, a week in the rue Vivienne
stops.date_confidence: attested to the first week of August 1814
stops.campa: A week in Paris with no money. Shelley goes out daily to raise something against expectations he does not yet control; the women read, and Mary keeps the journal that will become her first published book. The city in the summer after the abdication is full of foreign troops and the wreckage of twenty years of war, and none of the three shows any appetite for the sights. They wait for a remittance small enough that it can only be spent on foot. When it comes they walk out of the city eastward in the evening.
suggested_refs: The Hotel de Vienne, rue Vivienne, Paris, lodging of the eloping party
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817)

stops.name: Charenton, the ass sold and the mule bought
stops.date_confidence: attested; they reach Charenton about ten at night on 8 August and set out again the following morning
stops.campa: They come into Charenton at ten at night. The ass bought for the baggage proves useless and is sold in the morning; a mule is bought for ten Napoleons, and Mary rides it with the portmanteau strapped on while Shelley and Claire walk behind with a basket of provisions. They are dressed in black silk, which is what they own. In this order, a girl of sixteen on a mule and two walkers in mourning cloth, the party crosses a France still full of disbanded armies and villages burned in the winter's campaign.
stops.quote: Finding our ass useless, we sold it before we proceeded on our journey, and bought a mule, for ten Napoleons. About nine o'clock we departed. We were clad in black silk. I rode on the mule, which carried also our portmanteau; S*** and C*** followed, bringing a small basket of provisions.
stops.quote_source: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), Part I, France
suggested_refs: The road from Charenton to Gros Bois, first day of the walking journey
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), Project Gutenberg eBook 52790

stops.name: Neuchatel, the first sight of the Alps
stops.date_confidence: attested to mid-August 1814; the party is on the Swiss lakes by the 19th
stops.campa: Twelve days of walking, carts and river boats bring them across France to the Swiss lakes. Two leagues short of Neuchatel the Alps come up over the horizon, range behind black range, with the snow standing above everything, and Mary sets the sight down in the journal as an immensity the understanding has to labour to believe is part of the same earth she is standing on. It is her first mountain. Every glacier in the book she has not yet thought of will be measured against this afternoon on the road.
stops.quote: Two leagues from Neufchatel we saw the Alps: range after range of black mountains are seen extending one before the other, and far behind all, towering above every feature of the scene, the snowy Alps... Their immensity staggers the imagination, and so far surpasses all conception, that it requires an effort of the understanding to believe that they indeed form a part of the earth.
stops.quote_source: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), Part I, Switzerland
suggested_refs: The road above Lake Neuchatel, from which the Alpine chain first opens to the south
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), Project Gutenberg eBook 52790

stops.name: Brunnen, the house taken for six months and kept two days
stops.date_confidence: attested to the last week of August 1814
stops.campa: At Brunnen on the arm of Lake Lucerne they take rooms in an ugly new house on a six-month lease, pay in advance, and sit down to live cheaply and write: Shelley at a romance, Mary at a story called Hate. Two days later the purse is counted again. Twenty-eight pounds are left, not enough to stay and barely enough to go. They give up the lease, turn north for the cheapest road in Europe, and go down the Rhine by open boat among boatmen whose company disgusts all three of them, reading aloud for the length of the river.
suggested_refs: The Chateau of Brunnen on Lake Lucerne, leased and abandoned in three days
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817)
Wikipedia, 'History of a Six Weeks' Tour'

stops.name: Gravesend, put ashore in debt
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Rhine carries them past broken castles and vineyards to the Dutch ports, and the packet lands them at Gravesend with nothing left; the boatman will not put them ashore until he is paid, so Shelley goes up to London to borrow the fare from his wife while Mary and Claire sit in the boat. Six weeks have cost all three of them their families. Mary is seventeen and carrying a child that will not live. In three years this journal, with the Geneva letters and Shelley's Mont Blanc, will be printed as History of a Six Weeks' Tour.
suggested_refs: Gravesend, Kent, landing place of the returning elopement, 13 September 1814
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817)
Wikipedia, 'History of a Six Weeks' Tour'

stops.name: London, the child that lives twelve days
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A daughter is born two months early in lodgings the bailiffs are watching, and lives twelve days. Mary wakes to find her dead, and afterwards keeps dreaming the same dream: that the baby was only cold, that they rub it before the fire and it comes back to life. She writes the dream down on the nineteenth of March. She is seventeen, cut off by her father, sharing a house with her stepsister and a man who lectures them both on the freedom of the affections. Geneva is two summers off.
suggested_refs: Mary Shelley's journal entry of 19 March 1815, recording the dream of the revived infant

stops.name: Geneva, the two households meet at Secheron
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Claire, pregnant by Byron and pursuing him, brings the whole party to Switzerland: Mary, Shelley, the four-month-old William born at Bishopsgate in January, and Elise the Swiss nurse. They take rooms at Secheron on the lake Rousseau made famous, whose Julie Mary reads against its own shore. Byron arrives on the twenty-fifth with a young physician, having signed the deed of separation from Annabella Milbanke in April and left England for good with an infant daughter, Ada, behind him. The two households meet at the hotel and are not parted again for four months.
stops.quote: In the summer of 1816, we visited Switzerland, and became the neighbours of Lord Byron.
stops.quote_source: Mary Shelley, Author's Introduction to the 1831 edition of Frankenstein
suggested_refs: The Hotel d'Angleterre at Secheron, Geneva, where the Shelley party lodged before taking the lakeshore houses
sources: Polidori's diary, ed. W. M. Rossetti (1911)

stops.name: Villa Diodati, the ghost story proposed
stops.date_confidence: the proposal falls in the week after Byron takes the villa on 10 June 1816; no source fixes the day
stops.campa: Byron takes the Villa Diodati above the lake on the tenth of June, the Shelley party the Maison Chapuis five minutes below through the vineyard. The summer never comes. Tambora blew its mountain into the sky in the Indies the year before, and the ash makes a cold wet dark of June: rain for days, the lake white with squalls, everyone shut indoors. They read German ghost stories aloud in French and argue about galvanism, about whether the principle of life can be handled. Byron proposes that each of them write a ghost story. There are four in the room.
stops.quote: "We will each write a ghost story," said Lord Byron; and his proposition was acceded to. There were four of us.
stops.quote_source: Mary Shelley, Author's Introduction to the 1831 edition of Frankenstein
suggested_refs: The Villa Diodati at Cologny, rented by Byron from 10 June to 1 November 1816
Fantasmagoriana (1812), the French ghost-story collection read aloud at Diodati
sources: Mary Shelley's 1831 introduction to Frankenstein, Project Gutenberg eBook 42324
Polidori's diary, ed. W. M. Rossetti (1911)

stops.name: Villa Diodati, the waking dream
stops.date_confidence: attested to mid-June 1816; Donald Olson's 2011 astronomical reconstruction places the vision between two and three in the morning of 16 June
stops.campa: She cannot think of a story, and is asked each morning whether she has thought of one yet. After a night of talk about galvanism and the reanimation of a corpse she lies awake in the dark of the lakeside house and sees, with her eyes shut, a pale student kneeling beside the thing he has put together. The horror of it is that the man sleeps, and wakes, and it is standing at his bedside looking at him. In the morning she says she has found her story. She is eighteen. Polidori takes his own fragment from these nights and makes The Vampyre of it; his sister will raise Dante Gabriel and Christina Rossetti on the family's memory of this summer.
stops.quote: I saw--with shut eyes, but acute mental vision,--I saw the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together. I saw the hideous phantasm of a man stretched out, and then, on the working of some powerful engine, show signs of life, and stir with an uneasy, half vital motion.
stops.quote_source: Mary Shelley, Author's Introduction to the 1831 edition of Frankenstein
suggested_refs: Donald Olson's 2011 astronomical dating of the waking dream to 16 June 1816
John William Polidori, The Vampyre (1819), grown from the same contest
sources: Mary Shelley's 1831 introduction to Frankenstein, Project Gutenberg eBook 42324

stops.name: Chamonix, the valley in rain
stops.date_confidence: attested to late July 1816
stops.campa: In July the party crosses into the valley of Chamonix in rain, the pines torn open by avalanche tracks, the Arve loud in its gorge under a wall of ice. Shelley writes his lines on Mont Blanc here and signs himself atheist in Greek in the hotel books, which travellers copy and repeat across Europe. Mary looks at the same wall and takes a stage from it: the highest ground a man can climb to and still be found by what he has made. The mountain answers no one who stands under it.
suggested_refs: The hotel registers of Chamonix and Montanvert bearing Shelley's Greek signature
Percy Shelley, Mont Blanc, printed in History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817)
sources: History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817)

stops.name: Mer de Glace, the creature comes over the ice
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24-25 July 1816
stops.campa: They climb to Montenvers in the rain and come out over the Mer de Glace, a frozen sea broken into waves and crevasses, moving a foot a day and carrying the trees down with it. Mary crosses part of the ice. On this glacier she stages the meeting at the centre of her book: Victor Frankenstein climbing to be alone with his grief, and the creature coming over the ice with more than mortal speed to demand a hearing, and getting one. It is the only stretch of the novel where the made thing tells its own story from beginning to end.
suggested_refs: The Mer de Glace seen from the Montenvers belvedere, setting of Frankenstein chapter 10

stops.name: Bath, the winter of the two suicides
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1816
stops.campa: The party comes back from Geneva to Bath, where Claire's pregnancy by Byron can be hidden behind a false name and a hired room. Mary takes drawing lessons and writes the novel through the autumn. In October her half-sister Fanny Imlay leaves London, goes as far as Swansea, and takes laudanum in a room at the Mackworth Arms; Godwin and Shelley trace her a day too late, and Godwin insists on silence, so she is buried unclaimed. In December Harriet Shelley is taken out of the Serpentine, drowned and far gone in pregnancy.
suggested_refs: The Mackworth Arms Inn, Swansea, where Fanny Imlay died on the night of 9 October 1816
Bath, 5 Abbey Churchyard, lodgings of the Shelley party in the autumn of 1816

stops.name: St Mildred's, Bread Street: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Three weeks after the inquest on Harriet, Mary Godwin and Percy Shelley are married in the small church on Bread Street with Godwin and his wife standing as witnesses. The reconciliation is instant: the philosopher who wrote against marriage now informs his relations that his daughter has married the eldest son of a baronet. She signs the register as Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin for the last time. The marriage does not buy the children back. In March the Court of Chancery rules Shelley unfit to raise Harriet's son and daughter, and they are given to strangers.
suggested_refs: The parish register of St Mildred, Bread Street, 30 December 1816

stops.name: Albion House, Marlow: the fair copy finished
stops.date_confidence: the manuscript is finished in the spring of 1817 at Marlow, after most of the drafting at Bath through the previous winter; no exact day is recorded
stops.campa: At Marlow the household takes a damp long-leased house with a library and Mary finishes the book. Shelley reads it, makes it more Latinate in a hundred places, writes the preface in her voice and carries it round the trade, where it is refused twice. In the manuscript her creature teaches itself to be a person out of three books found in a portmanteau: Plutarch's lives of the great, Milton's Paradise Lost, and Goethe's Sorrows of Werther. In September a daughter is born and named Clara Everina, after the aunts Mary has never been allowed to meet.
suggested_refs: Albion House, West Street, Marlow
The Frankenstein notebooks in the Bodleian, showing Percy Shelley's hand in the margins

stops.name: Finsbury Square, three volumes without a name
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of January Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus is published in three volumes, anonymous, five hundred copies, from the Temple of the Muses on Finsbury Square by a firm that deals in remainders and the occult. The dedication is to William Godwin and the preface is Shelley's, so the reviewers hand the book to Shelley and scold it for its author's known opinions; Walter Scott praises it and makes the same assumption. Two months earlier the same season had brought out History of a Six Weeks' Tour, also unsigned. She is twenty.
stops.quote: And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper. I have an affection for it, for it was the offspring of happy days, when death and grief were but words, which found no true echo in my heart.
stops.quote_source: Mary Shelley, Author's Introduction to the 1831 edition of Frankenstein, written fifteen years after the first publication
suggested_refs: The 1818 title page, Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor and Jones, Finsbury Square
The Temple of the Muses bookshop on Finsbury Square
sources: Publication imprint of the 1818 first edition

segments.name: Italy, and the Graves of the Children

stops.name: Milan, the child sent to Venice
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The household crosses the Alps in March, meaning never to come back, and comes down to Milan, where they look at the cathedral daily and try for a villa on Lake Como that they cannot get. One thing is settled: Byron will take Allegra, his daughter by Claire, and raise her as his own, and will not have Claire anywhere near her. On the twenty-eighth of April the child, fifteen months old, is put into a coach for Venice with Elise the Swiss nurse and sent away. Claire has traded her daughter for a father's name. Mary keeps the household moving south.
suggested_refs: The Duomo of Milan and the Shelley lodgings of April 1818
The convent of Bagnacavallo, where Allegra was placed and where she died in 1822

stops.name: Venice, Clara dies on the road
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1818
stops.campa: In August Claire makes Shelley take her to Venice to see Allegra, and to keep the visit plausible he writes to Mary that she must come at once with both children, four hundred miles of late-summer road, though the baby is already sick. Mary travels day and night because the letter says come. Clara, one year old and dysenteric, begins to convulse on the last stage; the mother carries her into Venice, and while Shelley hunts a doctor the child dies in her arms. She is buried on the Lido. The journal goes almost silent for weeks.
suggested_refs: The Lido of Venice, burial place of Clara Everina Shelley, September 1818

stops.name: Naples, the registered child
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 1818-1819; the registration itself is dated 27 February 1819
stops.campa: The family winters at Naples with the bay under the windows, climbs Vesuvius by chair and mule, and walks the dug-out streets of Pompeii and Herculaneum. Mary is silent and Shelley writes his stanzas of dejection. In February a birth is registered at the city hall: Elena Adelaide Shelley, daughter of Percy and Mary Shelley, born the previous December. Mary was not pregnant. The child is left with foster parents, dies before she is eighteen months old, and no one who knows says whose she was. The household leaves Naples without mentioning her again.
suggested_refs: The Naples birth registration of Elena Adelaide Shelley, 27 February 1819
The excavations of Pompeii as the Shelleys saw them in 1819

stops.name: Rome, the death of Willmouse
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They come to Rome in March for the Holy Week and the ruins. Shelley writes in the baths of Caracalla, Mary draws in the galleries, and William, three and a half, learns Italian from the servants and is called Willmouse in the letters. In June the malaria season opens early. The boy sickens on the second, his father sits up with him sixty hours, and he dies on the seventh. Mary has buried three children in four years and is carrying none. The household is out of Rome within the week and she does not write in the journal for a month.
suggested_refs: The via del Corso lodgings of the Shelleys, spring 1819
Shelley's letters from Rome, June 1819

stops.name: The Protestant Cemetery, by the pyramid of Cestius
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1819
stops.campa: William is buried in the burying ground of strangers under the pyramid of Cestius, among cypresses where Keats will be laid two years later. Within three years the boy's father is brought here in a box and walled up a few yards off. Mary comes back to this ground for the rest of her travelling life. The grave itself is lost: the sexton's marks fail, and when the family later digs for the child's coffin they find the plot holds a stranger's body, so no one now knows which of the graves is his.
stops.quote: There I left the mortal remains of those beloved—my husband and my children, whose loss changed my whole existence, substituting, for happy peace and the interchange of deep-rooted affections, years of desolate solitude, and a hard struggle with the world...
stops.quote_source: Mary Shelley, Rambles in Germany and Italy (1844), Part I, Letter I, Brighton, 13 June 1840
suggested_refs: The Cimitero Acattolico, Rome, graves of William Shelley, Percy Bysshe Shelley and John Keats
sources: Rambles in Germany and Italy (1844), Project Gutenberg eBook 74280

stops.name: Florence, the son who lives
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The household moves to Florence for the birth, into rooms on the Lungarno above the river. On the twelfth of November a son is born and they name him Percy Florence for the city. He is her fourth child and the only one who will grow up. She is twenty-two and has been in mourning six months; the boy does not close that, but the journal starts again and the work with it. She is writing Valperga, a novel of fourteenth-century Tuscany, and when it is finished she gives it to her father to sell for his own debts.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Marini on the Lungarno, Florence, birthplace of Sir Percy Florence Shelley

stops.name: San Terenzo, the house in the water
stops.date_confidence: attested to the end of April 1822; one strand of the sources loosely dates the move to the summer
stops.campa: Days after the news that Allegra has died of typhus in her convent, the household is moved into Casa Magni at San Terenzo: a white arcaded house standing in the water with woods behind it and no road to the door. Mary hates it from the first week. The surf runs under the windows, the fishing people dance on the sand at night, there is no privacy anywhere, and two families and their servants are packed into rooms that open into one another. She is pregnant again and ill. Shelley has a new boat coming from Genoa and is happy.
suggested_refs: Casa Magni at San Terenzo, on the Bay of Lerici

stops.name: Casa Magni, the ice bath
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of June she miscarries and bleeds for seven hours while a doctor is fetched from a distance that cannot be covered in time. Shelley has ice brought up and sets her in it against every opinion in the room, and the bleeding stops. She is alive because he refuses to defer to the physicians. In the fortnight after, he begins seeing things in that house: a child rising out of the sea, a cloaked figure asking him how long he means to be content. He tells her that he has met himself on the terrace.
suggested_refs: Mary Shelley's later account of the miscarriage at Casa Magni, June 1822

stops.name: Livorno, the boat loaded for home
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Shelley sails the Don Juan down to Livorno with Edward Williams to meet Leigh Hunt, brought out from England to run a journal with Byron, and to settle the money for it. Mary, still weak, asks him not to go and cannot say why. In Livorno he sees Hunt for the last time and takes from him a volume of Keats, dead in Rome the year before. On the eighth he loads the boat for the run up the coast, ignores the advice to wait out the weather building to the west, and puts to sea about noon.
suggested_refs: The port of Livorno, from which the Don Juan sailed on 8 July 1822
sources: Trelawny, Recollections of the Last Days of Shelley and Byron

stops.name: The Gulf, off Viareggio: the squall
stops.date_confidence: attested; the position of the wreck itself is only approximately known
stops.campa: A squall comes down within an hour of their leaving, thick with rain, and the fishing boats run for shore. When it clears the Don Juan is gone with three men aboard. For ten days Mary and Jane Williams wait at Casa Magni, driving to Pisa and Livorno for news, holding to the story that the boat has been carried to Corsica. Trelawny comes back on the nineteenth and says nothing, and she reads it in his face. The bodies come ashore near Viareggio, Shelley's with the Keats folded back in the jacket pocket. She is twenty-four.
suggested_refs: The Gulf of La Spezia and the coast off Viareggio, where the Don Juan went down
sources: Trelawny, Recollections of the Last Days of Shelley and Byron

stops.name: Viareggio, the fire on the beach
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Quarantine law says a body out of the sea must be burned where it lies. Trelawny builds an iron furnace and brings the party down the sand: Byron, who swims out to a ship rather than watch the end of it, and Leigh Hunt, who stays in the carriage. The fire takes hours in the August heat. Trelawny puts his hand into it and pulls out an organ that will not burn. Mary is not there. The thing is fought over between Hunt and Trelawny, given to the widow at last, and she keeps it wrapped in paper for twenty-nine years.
suggested_refs: The beach at Viareggio and Trelawny's iron furnace, 16 August 1822
Louis Edouard Fournier's 1889 painting The Funeral of Shelley, a late invention of the scene
sources: Trelawny, Recollections of the Last Days of Shelley and Byron

stops.name: Genoa, the Journal of Sorrow at Albaro
stops.date_confidence: attested to late September 1822; she leaves Genoa in the last week of July 1823, about ten months later
stops.campa: She takes the upper floor of the Casa Negroto at Albaro and the Hunts take the lower: seven Hunt children below, a widow of twenty-five above who now has to earn. Byron is up the hill at the Casa Saluzzo and comes down often; she copies his cantos of Don Juan for money and hates the position it puts her in. Here she makes the fair copy of Valperga, and here she begins the notebook she calls her journal of sorrow, written for no reader, since the reader she wrote for is under the pyramid in Rome.
suggested_refs: Casa Negroto at Albaro, Genoa, shared with the Hunt family, 1822-1823
Mary Shelley's Journal of Sorrow, begun at Genoa in October 1822

stops.name: The Strand, back in her father's street
stops.date_confidence: attested to late August 1823; she leaves Genoa on 23-25 July and reaches London a month later
stops.campa: She lands in England in the last week of August with a boy of three and no income, and lodges in the Strand beside her father, who is bankrupt again. Sir Timothy Shelley, who has never met her and never will, offers terms for his grandson: an allowance advanced against the boy's future, no biography of his son, her husband's name kept out of print and hers with it. She has a famous book she is not credited for and the papers of a poet nobody yet rates, and no one else alive can read his hand.
suggested_refs: Godwin's lodgings in the Strand, 1823
The correspondence with Sir Timothy Shelley's solicitors over the allowance

stops.name: The English Opera House, the creature without lines
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Four days after landing she goes to the Lyceum to watch Presumption; or, the Fate of Frankenstein, in which the creature is played blue-grey and mute by Mr T. P. Cooke and the playbill gives the part as a blank dash. The house is full and the clergy are protesting in the street outside. The play runs, and the book runs behind it: five stage versions in three years, penny abridgements with woodcuts, and the beginning of the long slide by which the maker's name comes off the man and settles on the thing he made.
suggested_refs: The playbill of Presumption; or, the Fate of Frankenstein, English Opera House, 1823, listing the creature as a dash

stops.name: London, Posthumous Poems suppressed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1824; the pool gives no month for publication or for the suppression
stops.campa: She gathers Shelley's unpublished verse out of the notebooks, deciphering a hand written across itself in the margins of other poems and around the sketches, and brings out Posthumous Poems in an edition of five hundred. Sir Timothy stops it at once. The remaining copies are withdrawn and her allowance is made conditional on her printing nothing more of his son's while he lives. He lives another twenty-two years. That summer she moves out to Kentish Town to be near Jane Williams, the other widow of the boat.
suggested_refs: Posthumous Poems of Percy Bysshe Shelley (1824), suppressed by Sir Timothy Shelley
The Shelley notebooks she worked from, now in the Bodleian

stops.name: London, The Last Man
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1826; the pool gives the year only
stops.campa: She writes a novel in which a plague empties the world and one survivor walks through the ruins of Rome with a book and a dog. Its doomed idealist is Shelley and its poet-lord is Byron, and the last man is herself: the one left of a circle, keeping the record because there is no one else to keep it. The reviews are savage. The book sells poorly, goes out of print, and stays out for a century and more. She is twenty-eight and has outlived Shelley, Byron, Keats, Fanny, Harriet, Allegra and three of her four children.
suggested_refs: The Last Man (1826), three volumes, Henry Colburn

stops.name: St Pancras Old Church, her father laid beside her mother
stops.date_confidence: the pool attests the year 1836 and his age of eighty; the day of the funeral is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: William Godwin dies at eighty. He is the man who wrote that gratitude is no virtue and family no claim, and who then cut his daughter for two and a half years over an elopement conducted on his own published principles, while accepting the eloper's money. She has been supporting him out of her earnings for a decade. He is buried at St Pancras in the grave of Mary Wollstonecraft, the pair of them under one stone at last. Mary begins the memoir of him that he asked for, works at it for years, and never finishes it.
suggested_refs: The Godwin and Wollstonecraft grave at St Pancras Old Church, before the 1851 exhumation

stops.name: London, the collected Shelley for Moxon
stops.date_confidence: the commission is attested to 1838 and the Poetical Works appear in 1839; the pool gives no months
stops.campa: Edward Moxon pays her five hundred pounds to edit the collected Poetical Works. Sir Timothy, past eighty, permits notes and forbids a life, so she writes the life inside the notes: a prose essay before each year's poems giving the weather, the house, the illness, the quarrel, the occasion of the poem. The edition that makes Shelley a canonical English poet is hers: her texts, her dating, her account of a man the public will meet in the shape she has chosen for him. Trelawny calls it cowardice and never forgives the omissions.
suggested_refs: The Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley, ed. Mary Shelley, Edward Moxon, 1839, with her prefatory notes
sources: Publication history of the 1839 Poetical Works

stops.name: Sorrento, the bay seen again
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1843, on the second of the two continental journeys, which ran from June 1842 to September 1843
stops.campa: Twenty-four years after the winter of the registered child, she is back on the bay with her son and his Cambridge friends: the same mountain, the same dug-out streets, the crossing to Sorrento. She is forty-five and travelling with young men who want to see everything and be told what it is, and she lets them set the pace. The two journeys become Rambles in Germany and Italy, written for money and the last book she publishes, in which she names what this ground holds of hers and admits that the company never lets her stop beside it.
stops.quote: Now a new generation has sprung up; and, at the name of Italy, I grow young again in their enjoyments, and gladly prepare to share them.
stops.quote_source: Mary Shelley, Rambles in Germany and Italy (1844), Part I, Letter I, Brighton, 13 June 1840
suggested_refs: Rambles in Germany and Italy in 1840, 1842, and 1843 (1844), published under the name Mrs Shelley
sources: Rambles in Germany and Italy (1844), Project Gutenberg eBook 74280

stops.name: Chester Square, the last house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The last years are quiet and full of work: two more novels, the travel book, the blackmailers who turn up with Shelley letters to sell and have to be paid off, the son who comes into the baronetcy in 1844 and marries a woman devoted to the family's dead. From 1848 her right side fails by degrees, the headaches get worse, and she can no longer read for long. She dies at Chester Square at fifty-three, of what the doctors take for a tumour of the brain, having said that she wishes to lie with her mother.
suggested_refs: 24 Chester Square, Pimlico, the house of Sir Percy Florence and Lady Jane Shelley

stops.name: St Peter's, Bournemouth: the graves moved to her
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1851; the day of the interment is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: St Pancras churchyard is by now a slum with a railway cut coming through it, so the son and his wife will not put her there. They open her mother's grave and her father's, take up both coffins, and carry them down to St Peter's at Bournemouth, near the house the son has bought. Mary is laid between her parents in the vault, lying for the first time beside the woman who died eleven days after making her. The wish is honoured by breaking the graves that held it.
suggested_refs: The Shelley family vault at St Peter's Church, Bournemouth, holding Mary Shelley with William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft

stops.name: The writing desk opened a year after
stops.date_confidence: attested to the first anniversary of her death, February 1852; the room in which the desk was opened is not recorded in the sources consulted
stops.campa: On the first anniversary the son and his wife open her box desk. Inside are locks of her dead children's hair, a notebook she and Shelley wrote in together, and a copy of Adonais with one page folded round a silk parcel: ashes, and the dried remains of the organ Trelawny pulled out of the fire at Viareggio thirty years before. Jane, Lady Shelley, tells the story, and the family shrine at Boscombe is built on it. Later readers object that a heart burns like anything else and that what would not burn was more probably a liver.
suggested_refs: The copy of Adonais with the silk parcel, described in Jane, Lady Shelley's account of the desk
The Shelley relic room assembled at Boscombe Manor
